note: All data, names and figures are FICTIONAL. Not real market data, not investment advice.

cases.title: The double export
cases.boss_question: Did unit sales in {region} rise, fall or stay flat compared with the previous week?
cases.trap: The export was run twice, so some rows appear two times and inflate the total.
reference_steps: Count rows and compare with distinct order IDs
Remove duplicates using order_id plus date as the key
Check the row count dropped by the number of copies
Group by day and compare with the previous week
truth_statement_templates: After removing {n_dupes} duplicate rows, units in {region} changed {pct_change} versus the previous 7 days.
The raw total overstated sales by {n_dupes_units} units because of the double export.

wrong_paths.why: Copies are counted twice so the week looks stronger than it was.

wrong_paths.path: Delete every row that looks similar
wrong_paths.why: Two genuine orders with the same product and size are not duplicates; only the full key matters.

cases.title: The silent zeros
cases.boss_question: Are daily sales in {region} falling, recovering or flat this week?
cases.trap: A store whose till was offline exported 0 units instead of a blank, dragging the average down.
reference_steps: Sort units ascending and list the zeros
Check whether the zeros match store outage days or other sources
Treat confirmed outage zeros as missing
Compute the daily average over the days with data
truth_statement_templates: Daily average units were {avg_clean}, not {avg_raw}; {n_zero_days} zero days were outages, not real sales.
Sales in {region} are {direction} once outage days are excluded.

wrong_paths.why: The fake zeros pull the mean down and invent a decline.

wrong_paths.path: Fill zeros with the overall mean
wrong_paths.why: That invents sales on days nothing was recorded and hides the gap.

cases.title: Dollars and dong in one column
cases.boss_question: Is average revenue per order in {region} rising, falling or flat?
cases.trap: Revenue is recorded in two currencies and in thousands in some rows, so rows are not comparable.
reference_steps: Group by the currency column to see all values
Convert amounts to one currency using the stated fixed rate
Convert 'k' values to plain units
Recompute the average per order
truth_statement_templates: After converting to one currency, average revenue per order was {avg_clean} per order, {pct_change} versus last week.
{n_rows_converted} rows were in the second currency or in thousands.

wrong_paths.why: Small numbers in dollars and large numbers in local money are mixed, so the average means nothing.

wrong_paths.path: Convert only the currency, not the thousands
wrong_paths.why: Rows marked k are still 1000 times too small.

cases.title: Midnight in two time zones
cases.boss_question: Did sign-ups jump on {date} or was it a data artefact?
cases.trap: Dates arrive in mixed formats and one source uses UTC while the other uses local time, moving late-evening events to the next day.
reference_steps: Inspect date formats and the source column
Parse each source with the right format
Convert both sources to one time zone
Re-aggregate by day and compare
truth_statement_templates: After aligning time zones, sign-ups on {date} were {n_clean}, not {n_raw}; the apparent jump was a day boundary shift.
Dates in {n_formats} formats were parsed before grouping.

wrong_paths.path: Group by the raw date text
wrong_paths.why: Sorting text puts 10 Mar before 2 Mar and splits days.

wrong_paths.path: Assume all rows use the same time zone
wrong_paths.why: Evening events slip into the next day and create a fake spike.

cases.title: Hanoi, Ha Noi and hanoi
cases.boss_question: Which region sold the most units this week?
cases.trap: The same region is spelled several ways, so a group-by splits it and hides the real leader.
reference_steps: Group by region and read the list of names
Standardise case, spaces and spelling variants
Re-group and sort
Chart as a sorted bar with units
truth_statement_templates: {region_top} was the top region with {units_top} units after merging spelling variants.
{n_variants} spelling variants of {region_top} were merged.

wrong_paths.path: Pick the largest group in the raw list
wrong_paths.why: A region split across three spellings can rank below a smaller, cleanly spelled one.

wrong_paths.path: Merge regions that merely sound alike
wrong_paths.why: Only merge names that really are the same place.

cases.title: One extra zero
cases.boss_question: Will {commodity} prices rise, fall or stay flat this week?
cases.trap: One price is ten times its neighbours (an extra zero), while a separate, smaller jump is a genuine market move.
reference_steps: Plot the series as a line
Flag outliers with the IQR rule
Check the flagged points against neighbours and a second source
Fix the typo and keep the persistent real move
Read the trend from the cleaned series
truth_statement_templates: The {date_bad} value was an entry error (about 10x the neighbours) and was corrected.
The rise from {level_before} to {level_after} persisted for {n_days} days and is real.

wrong_paths.why: The persistent rise is real information and is removed with the typo.
A single wrong value makes the average and the chart useless.

cases.title: December is not a trend
cases.boss_question: Is demand in {region} really recovering, or is it just the usual seasonal pattern?
cases.trap: A repeating seasonal peak looks like growth when compared with the preceding off-season period.
reference_steps: Chart at least two years on the same axis
Compare with the same period last year
Estimate the typical seasonal swing
Report the year-on-year change as the trend
truth_statement_templates: Sales are {pct_mom} versus last month but {pct_yoy} versus the same month last year.
About {pct_season} of the rise matches the normal seasonal swing.

wrong_paths.why: The previous month is seasonally low, so any month looks like growth.

wrong_paths.path: Fit a straight line to the whole series
wrong_paths.why: The line ignores the repeating pattern and misleads about direction.

cases.title: Winner by group, loser overall
cases.boss_question: Which checkout version converts better, A or B?
cases.trap: Variant B converts better inside both device groups but looks worse overall because it received mostly mobile traffic.
reference_steps: Compute conversion by variant
Split by device and recompute
Compare variants inside each device
Report the like-for-like result and the traffic mix difference
truth_statement_templates: B converts better than A on desktop ({a_desktop} vs {b_desktop}) and on mobile ({a_mobile} vs {b_mobile}).
The overall gap is reversed because the device mix differs between variants.

wrong_paths.why: The overall rate reflects a different mix of devices, not the quality of the page.
Check why the mix differs; if assignment was not random, neither view is final.

cases.title: Three customers is not a trend
cases.boss_question: Is satisfaction in {category} better or worse than last month?
cases.trap: A category with very few responses swings wildly and looks like a big change.
reference_steps: Count responses per category
Mark groups below a minimum count
Compare the large groups only, or pool several months
Report counts with each rate
truth_statement_templates: {category} had only {n} responses, so a change of {pct_change} is within normal noise.
Categories with at least {n_min} responses were stable.

wrong_paths.why: Tiny groups sit at the top and bottom of any ranking by chance.
Say it is uncertain instead of hiding it.

cases.title: Ads and sales move together
cases.boss_question: Did the ad campaign cause the sales rise in {region}?
cases.trap: Ad spend and sales both rise because of a third factor (a holiday season), so the link is not causal.
reference_steps: Chart spend and sales over time
Check for a common driver such as season or price promotion
Compare treated and untreated regions or periods
Word the finding as an association unless a test exists
truth_statement_templates: Ad spend and sales are associated (r = {r}), but a holiday explains much of the rise.
Regions without the campaign rose by {pct_control}, so the campaign effect is at most {pct_effect}.

wrong_paths.path: Say the campaign caused the rise
wrong_paths.why: Without a comparison group, a coincident holiday explains the same pattern.
There is a link; it just cannot be called causal from this data.

cases.title: The fraud alarm that cries wolf
cases.boss_question: The risk model flags an account. Is it likely a real default?
cases.trap: The model is accurate, but defaults are rare, so most flags are false alarms.
reference_steps: State the base rate of default
Build a table of flagged and not flagged by real outcome
Compute the share of flags that are real
Report precision, not just model accuracy
truth_statement_templates: Only {precision} of flagged accounts actually default because defaults are rare ({base_rate}).
Out of {n_flags} flags, {n_true} were real defaults.

wrong_paths.path: Treat a flag as a 90% chance of default
wrong_paths.why: Accuracy figures ignore how rare the event is.
It still raises the odds; use it as a screen, not a verdict.

cases.title: Only the survivors answered
cases.boss_question: How risky is our loan book, based on the default rate?
cases.trap: Closed and defaulted accounts were removed from the export, so the book looks safer than it is.
reference_steps: Check the status column for closed or charged-off values
Ask what was removed and request the full history
Build cohorts by origination month and track defaults over time
Report the default rate with and without closed accounts
truth_statement_templates: The export only contained {n_open} open accounts; {n_closed} closed accounts were missing.
Including closed accounts, the default rate is {rate_full}, not {rate_open}.

wrong_paths.path: Compute the default rate from the file
wrong_paths.why: Defaulted accounts are the ones that were removed.

wrong_paths.path: Assume the missing accounts all defaulted
wrong_paths.why: Many closed accounts were simply repaid; get the real records.

cases.title: The perfect date range
cases.boss_question: A colleague says {series} has risen {pct_cherry} this month. Is that fair?
cases.trap: The quoted rise starts at a temporary low and ends at a temporary high; over the full period the series is flat.
reference_steps: Ask for the start and end dates behind the claim
Chart the full period
Compare several windows
State the change over a window chosen before looking
truth_statement_templates: The quoted rise holds only for {window_cherry}; over the full period the change was {pct_full}.
Different windows gave results from {low} to {high}.

wrong_paths.why: It is real but selected to look good.
Say the window is arbitrary and show the full picture.

cases.title: The chart that shouts
cases.boss_question: Make a chart of sales for the board. Does {region} outperform the others?
cases.trap: A bar chart whose axis starts at a high value makes a 3% difference look enormous.
reference_steps: Aggregate units by region
Build a bar chart with the Y-axis starting at zero
Sort the bars and add units and a clear title
State the real size of the difference
truth_statement_templates: {region} sold {pct_gap} more than the next region, a modest difference.
With a zero-based axis the bars look similar, which matches the data.

wrong_paths.path: Truncate the axis to show differences clearly
wrong_paths.why: Truncation makes small gaps look huge and misleads the board.
Pies make small differences harder to see, not more honest.

cases.title: Customers in two lists
cases.boss_question: How many unique customers bought in {region} this month?
cases.trap: Customers who bought through both web and app appear in both channel lists, so adding the lists overstates unique customers.
reference_steps: Count customers in each channel
Find customers present in both
Count unique customer IDs across channels
Check parts versus total
truth_statement_templates: There were {n_unique} unique customers, not {n_sum}; {n_overlap} used both channels.
Channel totals add to more than the true total.

wrong_paths.path: Add the web and app counts
wrong_paths.why: Customers who used both are counted twice.
That ignores customers who bought only through the other one.

cases.title: The half-finished Friday
cases.boss_question: Did sign-ups fall sharply on the last day, and should we panic?
cases.trap: The last day in the export is incomplete, so it looks like a crash.
reference_steps: Check export time versus end of day
Compare the last day's volume to a normal day at the same hour
Exclude or flag the partial day
Report the trend on complete days
truth_statement_templates: The final day was a partial day (exported at {export_time}); the trend on complete days was {direction}.
Excluding the partial day, average sign-ups were {avg_complete}.

wrong_paths.path: Report a collapse on the last day
wrong_paths.why: The records had not arrived yet.

wrong_paths.path: Delete the last day without saying so
wrong_paths.why: Note that data was excluded and why.

cases.title: Is a 7-point lift real?
cases.boss_question: Variant B looks better. Should we roll it out?
cases.trap: A visible difference may still be random; significance depends on the sample size and the p-value.
reference_steps: Remove test accounts
Check the groups are similar in size
Compute conversion per variant
Run the significance test and read the p-value with the effect size
Recommend roll out only if the difference is meaningful and significant
truth_statement_templates: B converts {rate_b} versus {rate_a} for A (p = {p}); the result is {sig_word}.
The effect is {diff_points} points; the interval ranges from {ci_low} to {ci_high}.

wrong_paths.why: Without a significance check the gap may be luck.

wrong_paths.path: Say p = 0.04 means a 96% chance B is better
wrong_paths.why: A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

cases.title: Stop the test now, it's winning
cases.boss_question: The test hit p < 0.05 on day 3 of a 14-day plan. Can we stop and ship?
cases.trap: Checking a test repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives.
reference_steps: Review the planned sample size and duration
Compute how many looks were taken
Treat early significance as provisional
Wait for the planned sample, or use a sequential method
truth_statement_templates: The test planned {n_plan} users per variant but had {n_now}; the early result is provisional.
With {n_looks} looks, the chance of at least one false positive is far above 5%.

wrong_paths.why: Repeated looks make false winners common.
The data is fine; it is the stopping rule that is not.

cases.title: Too few users to tell
cases.boss_question: The new button shows +1 point, but the test only had a few hundred users. What do we know?
cases.trap: The test is too small to detect a small effect, so 'no significant difference' does not mean 'no difference'.
reference_steps: Compute the required users per variant for the target lift
Compare with the actual sample
Report the result as inconclusive
Recommend running longer or accepting a bigger minimum lift
truth_statement_templates: The test had {n_actual} users per variant but needed about {n_needed} to detect {lift}.
The result is inconclusive, not negative.

wrong_paths.path: Conclude the button has no effect
wrong_paths.why: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence in a small test.
The interval includes zero.

cases.title: Where do customers leave?
cases.boss_question: Which step of the sign-up flow should we fix first?
cases.trap: Raw counts hide which step loses the largest share; the biggest percentage drop is the best place to look.
reference_steps: Order steps and count users per step
Compute step-to-step conversion
Find the largest proportional drop
Check that the last day is complete
Segment the weak step by device or source
truth_statement_templates: The biggest drop is from {step_a} to {step_b} ({conv_step}).
Overall conversion from visit to purchase is {conv_total}.

wrong_paths.path: Fix the step with the largest absolute drop
wrong_paths.why: The first step always loses the most users in raw numbers.
That makes late steps look worse than they are.

cases.title: New users are not loyal users
cases.boss_question: Is customer retention improving?
cases.trap: Overall active users grow because of new sign-ups while every new cohort retains worse than the last.
reference_steps: Define a cohort by sign-up month
Compute weeks since sign-up for each event
Build a retention table by cohort
Compare cohorts at the same age
truth_statement_templates: Week-4 retention fell from {ret_old} to {ret_new} across cohorts, although total active users grew.
Growth is driven by new sign-ups, not stickiness.

wrong_paths.why: New sign-ups hide churn.
Older cohorts have had more time to fall; compare at the same age.

cases.title: The average customer does not exist
cases.boss_question: Our average basket is flat. Is anything changing?
cases.trap: A flat average hides two segments moving in opposite directions.
reference_steps: Compute the average basket overall
Segment by customer type or channel
Compare each segment over time
Report segment sizes and changes
truth_statement_templates: The overall average is flat, but {segment_a} rose {pct_a} while {segment_b} fell {pct_b}.
Segment sizes were {n_a} and {n_b}.

wrong_paths.why: The movement cancels out in the average.
Small segments are noisy; keep a few meaningful ones.

cases.title: Why did revenue fall?
cases.boss_question: Revenue fell {pct_drop} this week. Why?
cases.trap: A total decline is caused by one narrow part (one region and product); the first plausible reason is not the full explanation.
reference_steps: Confirm the drop is real (not a data issue)
Split by region, then product, then channel
Find the part explaining most of the change
Check that the finding accounts for the whole drop
truth_statement_templates: {region} {product} explains {share_explained} of the decline.
Other regions were within normal variation.

wrong_paths.why: It is a story, not a finding.
A region-level drop may still hide a single product.

cases.title: The fix that fixed nothing
cases.boss_question: We ran a promotion in the 5 weakest shops and sales rose. Did it work?
cases.trap: Shops chosen for being the worst tend to improve next period even with no action.
reference_steps: Check how the shops were chosen
Look at several earlier periods
Compare with similar untreated shops
Estimate the effect beyond the natural rebound
truth_statement_templates: The 5 treated shops rose {pct_treated}, but similar untreated weak shops rose {pct_control}.
Most of the rise matches a natural rebound.

wrong_paths.why: Extreme results are partly luck and tend to move toward the average.
It did not; the effect is simply unproven.

cases.title: The customers who vanished
cases.boss_question: What is average balance by customer segment?
cases.trap: Customer IDs differ in format between the two tables, so a join silently drops customers.
reference_steps: Compare distinct keys in both tables
Standardise keys (trim spaces, leading zeros)
Join and compare the row count with the original
Recompute by segment
truth_statement_templates: After fixing key formats, {n_matched} of {n_total} accounts matched instead of {n_matched_raw}.
Average balance for {segment} was {avg_clean}.

wrong_paths.path: Use the joined table as is
wrong_paths.why: Missing customers are not random, so the averages are biased.
Names are not unique or stable.

cases.title: Staff signed up too
cases.boss_question: What is the conversion rate for new users this week?
cases.trap: Internal and test accounts convert at unusual rates and distort the metric.
reference_steps: Scan user IDs and emails for test patterns
Check unusual activity per user
Filter out confirmed test accounts and record the rule
Recompute the conversion rate
truth_statement_templates: After removing {n_test} test accounts, conversion was {rate_clean}, not {rate_raw}.
The exclusion rule was: {rule}.

wrong_paths.why: Test accounts are not customers.
A real power user is not a test account.

cases.title: The rows named Total
cases.boss_question: What was total revenue last month?
cases.trap: Subtotal and repeated header rows sit inside the data, so a column sum counts some rows twice.
reference_steps: Scan for text in number columns
Filter out repeated headers and total rows
Sum the remaining rows
Reconcile with the file's own grand total
truth_statement_templates: Revenue was {rev_clean}, not {rev_raw}; {n_subtotals} subtotal rows and {n_headers} repeated headers were removed.
The cleaned sum matches the grand total in the file.

wrong_paths.why: Subtotals are included, inflating revenue.

wrong_paths.path: Remove every row with a missing region
wrong_paths.why: Some real rows may have a blank region.

cases.title: Refunds are not errors
cases.boss_question: What was net revenue in {region}, and did returns rise?
cases.trap: Negative amounts are refunds that reduce revenue; cancelled orders are different and should not count as sales.
reference_steps: List negative amounts and statuses
Separate refunds from cancellations
Compute gross, refunds and net revenue
Compare the refund rate with the previous period
truth_statement_templates: Gross revenue was {gross}, refunds {refunds} and net {net}.
The refund rate moved from {rate_old} to {rate_new}.

wrong_paths.why: That overstates revenue.
They never completed.

cases.title: The file that stopped in September
cases.boss_question: How did sales in the full year compare with last year?
cases.trap: The export stopped at a row limit, so the last part of the year is missing.
reference_steps: Check the first and last dates
Check the row count for a round number
Request a complete export or limit conclusions to the covered period
Compare like periods only
truth_statement_templates: The data ends on {last_date} at exactly {n_rows} rows; the comparison only covers {covered}.
A complete export is needed for a full-year claim.

wrong_paths.path: Compare the partial year to the full year
wrong_paths.why: It will look like a collapse.
State the assumption or ask for the data.

cases.title: Prices from a messy scrape
cases.boss_question: Is the rival really cheaper than us on {item}?
cases.trap: Scraped prices mix pack sizes, currencies and promo labels, so raw prices are not comparable.
reference_steps: Standardise item names
Convert prices to one currency
Convert to price per unit (per kg or per piece)
Handle missing and promo prices
Compare medians
truth_statement_templates: Per unit, the rival is {pct_diff} cheaper on {item} (median of {n} listings).
{n_excluded} listings were excluded for missing price.

wrong_paths.why: A bigger pack costs more but not per unit.
A few extreme listings shift the mean; use the median.

cases.title: The full rescue
cases.boss_question: We need a reliable weekly sales figure for {region} for the board. Can you provide it?
cases.trap: One file has several defects at once: duplicates, typos, zeros that mean missing, and an incomplete last day.
reference_steps: Audit: row counts, distinct keys, zeros, date range
Remove duplicates
Standardise region names
Treat outage zeros as missing
Exclude the partial last day
Aggregate, compare with last week and log the assumptions
truth_statement_templates: After {n_steps} cleaning steps, weekly units in {region} were {value}, {pct_change} versus last week.
Defects found: {defect_list}.

wrong_paths.why: The remaining defects still move the answer.
Real variation was removed, making the data look too smooth.

cases.title: Two axes, one story
cases.boss_question: Does the exchange rate drive our raw material cost?
cases.trap: A dual-axis chart with hand-picked scales makes two unrelated series look tightly linked.
reference_steps: Plot each series on its own chart
Index both series to 100 at the same start date
Compute the correlation over several windows
State that the link is an association
truth_statement_templates: Indexed to 100, the two series diverged by {gap} points after {date}.
The apparent link in the dual-axis chart depended on the axis scales.

wrong_paths.why: The scales were chosen to line the series up.
Indexing shows partial co-movement; just no proof of cause.

cases.title: The average that describes nobody
cases.boss_question: What is the typical ticket resolution time?
cases.trap: Resolution times are strongly skewed; a few very long tickets drag the mean far above the typical time.
reference_steps: Draw a histogram of resolution times
Compare mean and median
Report the median and a high percentile
Segment slow tickets by category
truth_statement_templates: The median resolution time was {median}, while the mean was {mean} because of {n_long} very long tickets.
Slow tickets cluster in {category}.

wrong_paths.why: It describes neither the typical nor the slow tickets.
They are real and important.
